{{Short description|Conversion of a matrix or a tensor to a vector}}
{{other uses|Vectorization (disambiguation){{!}}Vectorization}}

In [[mathematics]], especially in [[linear algebra]] and [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix theory]], the '''vectorization''' of a [[matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] is a [[linear transformation]] which converts the matrix into a [[vector (mathematics and physics)|vector]]. Specifically, the vectorization of a {{nowrap|''m'' × ''n''}} matrix ''A'', denoted vec(''A''), is the {{nowrap|''mn'' × 1}} column vector obtained by stacking the columns of the matrix ''A'' on top of one another:
<math display="block">\operatorname{vec}(A) = [a_{1,1}, \ldots, a_{m,1}, a_{1,2}, \ldots, a_{m,2}, \ldots, a_{1,n}, \ldots, a_{m,n}]^\mathrm{\top}</math>
Here, <math>a_{i,j}</math> represents the element in the ''i''-th row and ''j''-th column of ''A'', and the superscript <math>{}^\mathrm{\top}</math> denotes the [[transpose]]. In other words, vec(''A'') is a vector containing the entries of ''A'' in [[Row- and column-major order|column-major]] order.

Vectorization expresses, through coordinates, the [[isomorphism]] <math>\mathbf{R}^{m \times n} \cong \mathbf{R}^{mn}</math> between these (i.e., of matrices and vectors) as vector spaces.

For example, for the 2×2 matrix <math>A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}</math>, the vectorization is <math>\operatorname{vec}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} a \\ c \\ b \\ d \end{bmatrix}</math>.

The connection between the vectorization of ''A'' and the vectorization of its transpose is given by the [[commutation matrix]].

==Compatibility with Kronecker products==

The vectorization is frequently used together with the [[Kronecker product]] to express [[matrix multiplication]] as a linear transformation on matrices. In particular,
<math display="block"> \operatorname{vec}(ABC) = (C^\mathrm{\top}\otimes A) \operatorname{vec}(B) </math>
for matrices ''A'', ''B'', and ''C'' of dimensions ''k''×''l'', ''l''×''m'', and ''m''×''n''.<ref group="note" name="RowMajor">The identity for row-major vectorization is <math> \operatorname{vec}(ABC) = (A \otimes C^\mathrm{\top})\operatorname{vec}(B)</math>.
</ref> For example, if <math> \operatorname{ad}_A(X) = AX-XA</math> (the [[adjoint endomorphism]] of the [[Lie algebra]] {{nowrap|gl(''n'', '''C''')}} of all ''n''×''n'' matrices with [[complex number|complex]] entries), then <math>\operatorname{vec}(\operatorname{ad}_A(X)) = (A \otimes I_n - I_n \otimes A^\mathrm{\top}) \text{vec}(X)</math>, where <math>I_n</math> is the ''n''×''n'' [[identity matrix]].

There are two other useful formulations:
<math display="block"> \begin{align}
\operatorname{vec}(ABC) &= (I_n\otimes AB)\operatorname{vec}(C) = (C^\mathrm{\top}B^\mathrm{\top}\otimes I_k) \operatorname{vec}(A) \\
\operatorname{vec}(AB) &= (I_m \otimes A) \operatorname{vec}(B) = (B^\mathrm{\top}\otimes I_k) \operatorname{vec}(A)
\end{align}</math>

If ''B'' is a [[Diagonal matrix|diagonal matrix]] (i.e., <math display='inline'>B = \operatorname{diag}(b_1, \dots, b_n)</math>), the vectorization can be written using the column-wise Kronecker product <math display="inline">\ast</math> (see [[Khatri–Rao product|Khatri-Rao product]]) and the [[Main diagonal|main diagonal]] <math display="inline">b = \begin{bmatrix} b_1, \dots, b_n \end{bmatrix}^\mathrm \top</math> of ''B'':
<math display="block"> \operatorname{vec}(ABC) = (C^\mathrm{\top} \ast A) b </math>

More generally, it has been shown that vectorization is a [[Adjoint functors|self-adjunction]] in the monoidal closed structure of any category of matrices.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=H. D. |last1=Macedo |first2=J. N. |last2=Oliveira |title=Typing Linear Algebra: A Biproduct-oriented Approach |journal=Science of Computer Programming |volume=78 |issue=11 |year=2013 |pages=2160–2191 |doi=10.1016/j.scico.2012.07.012 |arxiv=1312.4818 |s2cid=9846072 }}</ref>

==Compatibility with Hadamard products==

Vectorization is an [[algebra homomorphism]] from the space of {{nowrap|''n'' × ''n''}} matrices with the [[Hadamard product (matrices)|Hadamard]] (entrywise) product to '''C'''<sup>''n''<sup>2</sup></sup> with its Hadamard product:
<math display="block">\operatorname{vec}(A \circ B) = \operatorname{vec}(A) \circ \operatorname{vec}(B) .</math>

==Compatibility with inner products==

Vectorization is a [[unitary transformation]] from the space of ''n''×''n'' matrices with the [[Matrix norm#Frobenius norm|Frobenius]] (or [[Hilbert–Schmidt operator|Hilbert–Schmidt]]) [[inner product]] to '''C'''<sup>''n''<sup>2</sup></sup>:
<math display="block">\operatorname{tr}(A^\dagger B) = \operatorname{vec}(A)^\dagger \operatorname{vec}(B),</math>
where the superscript <sup>†</sup> denotes the [[conjugate transpose]].

==Vectorization as a linear sum==

The matrix vectorization operation can be written in terms of a linear sum. Let '''X''' be an {{nowrap|''m'' × ''n''}} matrix that we want to vectorize, and let '''e'''<sub>''i''</sub> be the ''i''-th canonical basis vector for the ''n''-dimensional space, that is <math display="inline">\mathbf{e}_i=\left[0,\dots,0,1,0,\dots,0\right]^\mathrm{T}</math>. Let '''B'''<sub>''i''</sub> be a {{nowrap|(''mn'') × ''m''}} block matrix defined as follows:
<math display="block">
\mathbf{B}_i = \begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{0} \\
\vdots \\
\mathbf{0} \\
\mathbf{I}_m \\
\mathbf{0} \\
\vdots \\
\mathbf{0}
\end{bmatrix}
= \mathbf{e}_i \otimes \mathbf{I}_m
</math>

'''B'''<sub>''i''</sub> consists of ''n'' block matrices of size {{nowrap|''m'' × ''m''}}, stacked column-wise, and all these matrices are all-zero except for the ''i''-th one, which is a {{nowrap|''m'' × ''m''}} identity matrix '''I'''<sub>''m''</sub>.

Then the vectorized version of '''X''' can be expressed as follows:
<math display="block">\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{X}) = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{B}_i \mathbf{X} \mathbf{e}_i</math>

Multiplication of '''X''' by '''e'''<sub>''i''</sub> extracts the ''i''-th column, while multiplication by '''B'''<sub>''i''</sub> puts it into the desired position in the final vector.

Alternatively, the linear sum can be expressed using the [[Kronecker product]]:
<math display="block">\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{X}) = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{e}_i \otimes \mathbf{X} \mathbf{e}_i</math>

==Half-vectorization==

For a [[symmetric matrix]] ''A'', the vector vec(''A'') contains more information than is strictly necessary, since the matrix is completely determined by the symmetry together with the [[lower triangular matrix|lower triangular]] portion, that is, the {{nowrap|''n''(''n'' + 1)/2}} entries on and below the [[main diagonal]]. For such matrices, the '''half-vectorization''' is sometimes more useful than the vectorization. The half-vectorization, vech(''A''), of a symmetric {{nowrap|''n'' × ''n''}} matrix ''A'' is the {{nowrap|''n''(''n'' + 1)/2 × 1}} column vector obtained by vectorizing only the lower triangular part of ''A'':
<math display="block"> \operatorname{vech}(A) = [A_{1,1}, \ldots, A_{n,1}, A_{2,2}, \ldots, A_{n,2}, \ldots, A_{n-1,n-1}, A_{n,n-1}, A_{n,n}]^\mathrm{\top}.</math>

For example, for the 2×2 matrix <math>A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ b & d \end{bmatrix}</math>, the half-vectorization is <math>\operatorname{vech}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} a \\ b \\ d \end{bmatrix}</math>.

There exist unique matrices transforming the half-vectorization of a matrix to its vectorization and vice versa called, respectively, the [[duplication matrix]] and the [[elimination matrix]].

==Programming language==
Programming languages that implement matrices may have easy means for vectorization.
In [[Matlab]]/[[GNU Octave]] a matrix <code>A</code> can be vectorized by <code>A(:)</code>.
[[GNU Octave]] also allows vectorization and half-vectorization with <code>vec(A)</code> and <code>vech(A)</code> respectively. [[Julia (programming language)|Julia]] has the <code>vec(A)</code> function as well.
In [[Python (programming language)|Python]] [[NumPy]] arrays implement the <code>flatten</code> method,<ref group="note" name="RowMajor"/> while in [[R programming language|R]] the desired effect can be achieved via the <code>c()</code> or <code>as.vector()</code> functions or, more efficiently, by removing the dimensions attribute of a matrix <code>A</code> with <code>dim(A) <- NULL</code>. In [[R programming language|R]], function <code>vec()</code> of package 'ks' allows vectorization and function <code>vech()</code> implemented in both packages 'ks' and 'sn' allows half-vectorization.<ref>{{cite web |first=Tarn |last=Duong |date=2018 |title=ks: Kernel Smoothing |work=R package version 1.11.0 |url=https://cran.r-project.org/package=ks }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |first=Adelchi |last=Azzalini |date=2017 |title=The R package 'sn': The Skew-Normal and Related Distributions such as the Skew-t |work=R package version 1.5.1 |url=https://cran.r-project.org/package=sn }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |first=Hrishikesh D. |last=Vinod |title=Hands-on Matrix Algebra Using R: Active and Motivated Learning with Applications |location=Singapore |publisher=World Scientific |year=2011 |isbn=978-981-4313-69-8 |chapter=Simultaneous Reduction and Vec Stacking |pages=233–248 |via=[[Google Books]] |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=oXzkJwutS1UC&pg=PA233 }}</ref>

==Applications==
Vectorization is used in [[matrix calculus]] and its applications in establishing e.g., moments of random vectors and matrices, asymptotics, as well as Jacobian and Hessian matrices.<ref>{{cite book
|last1=Magnus |first1=Jan |last2=Neudecker |first2=Heinz |title=Matrix differential calculus with applications in statistics and econometrics |publisher=John Wiley |location=New York |year=2019 |isbn=978-1-119-54120-2 }}</ref>
It is also used in local sensitivity and statistical diagnostics.<ref>{{Cite journal| last1=Liu|first1=Shuangzhe| last2=Leiva|first2=Victor| last3=Zhuang|first3=Dan| last4=Ma|first4=Tiefeng| last5=Figueroa-Zúñiga|first5=Jorge I.| date=March 2022|title=Matrix differential calculus with applications in the multivariate linear model and its diagnostics | journal=Journal of Multivariate Analysis| language=en| volume=188| article-number=104849| doi=10.1016/j.jmva.2021.104849 | doi-access=free}}</ref>
